newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- DEC 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- DEC 11.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--Farmers and government both have reached the limits of tolerance as six billion drachmas in exports are lost daily. Following the government's restatement of its intention yesterday to not give in, farmers said they would continue their blockade for the 14th day but there were reports than an increasing number were willing to dismantle barricades and go home.

Prime Minister Costas Simits leaves for his five-day visit to The Hague and Dublin today. In his absence, five ministers will run the show. At the Cabinet meeting yesterday, Simitis admitted that not all of ruling party PASOK supported the government's policy.
--Pensioners calling for parity with current wages yesterday met with Simitis after standing in the rain for two hours. Talks will continue at the labour and social security ministry next year.
--Turkish businessmen attending a two-day business cooperation council in Athens stress the only way out for the region is economic cooperation, and criticised wasteful defence spending.

--The European Union is expected to have its say on the farmers' blockades at tomorrow's Council of Ministers with Germany requesting Greece's explanation of the problems that have begun to arise in European markets. Britain's Foreign Office, meanwhile, has issued a travel advisory.
--Ten changes to wages and pensions are in the pipeline: among those are increases in bonuses to teachers, wage increases for judicial officials and tax cuts for tax and customs officials.

--There is hope for a de-escalation of the crisis on the roads, despite the reactions from Larissa farmers. Road blocks in other regions have been relaxed and the government hopes to gradually reduce and contain the road blocks to the Thessaly region.

--Public servants get more bad news: family benefits will be cut for those already receiving bonuses from the state or private sector, meaning a loss of up to 24,000 drachmas a month. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
